name: Voltage testers (non-contact pens and two-pole testers)
summary: Pocket tools that show whether a wire or socket is live: non-contact pens sense AC through the insulation but never prove a circuit dead; two-pole testers touch the conductors and show the voltage.
uses: Non-contact pens beep or glow near live AC wiring, sockets and cords. HSE says use them to spot live equipment, never to prove it dead (HSE GS38; Klein NCVT7; Fluke 1AC II)
A silent pen is not proof of dead: shielded cable, grounded conduit, distance, an insulated user, weak batteries, interference or a non-sine waveform can hide live AC (Klein NCVT7; Fluke 1AC II)
Most pens don't detect DC, so solar panels, battery banks, EV packs and inverter DC wiring read nothing (Klein NCVT7; Fluke pens)
For DC use only a two-pole tester or meter marked for DC and for more than the system's voltage; EV packs and big arrays are for trained people (Fluke T-series; HSE GS38)
Two-pole testers touch two conductors; Fluke's T-series show AC and DC. Fluke says a voltmeter or two-pole detector is needed to confirm no hazardous voltage (Fluke T-series; Fluke 1AC II)
Never use one above its marked voltage: 1,000 V on the pens here, 690 V on Fluke's two-pole T-series (Klein NCVT7; Fluke T-series)
identify: Non-contact pens are pen-sized, with a plastic tip that lights up and a beeper. The Fluke 1AC II gives a double flash every 2 seconds (VoltBeat) to show it is on and working, glows steadily at the tip near AC, and the North American models cover 90 to 1,000 V AC, the LAC low-voltage model 20 to 90 V (Fluke 1AC II). The Klein NCVT7 shows green when it finds nothing (voltage could still be present), blue for a weak signal and red for a strong one, over 12 to 1,000 V AC (Klein NCVT7). Two-pole testers have two probes joined by a fixed lead and a row of lights or a screen showing voltage steps, AC or DC; Fluke's T90 to T150 read from 6 or 12 V up to 690 V and are built to EN 61243-3 (Fluke T-series). Read the markings: the maximum voltage and a CAT rating. CAT II is for appliances and portable tools plugged into the installation, CAT III for panels, socket outlets and fixed wiring, CAT IV for the source of the installation such as meters and primary protection (HSE GS38). Ontario requires CAT III and IV testers to be approved and marked, certified to a standard such as CSA C22.2 No. 1010 or No. 231.0 (ESA Flash 19-03-FL); the NCVT7 is certified to CSA C22.2 No. 61010-1 (Klein NCVT7). Good probes have finger guards and no more than 4 mm of bare tip (HSE GS38).
test: Live, dead, live, every time. 1. Power: fit fresh batteries of the marked type. On the Fluke 1AC II the VoltBeat flash stops when the batteries get low; don't use it if it isn't flashing (Fluke 1AC II). The Klein NCVT7 switches itself off on a low battery (Klein NCVT7). 2. Look it over: a cracked case or tip, or damaged leads, mean don't use it (Fluke 1AC II; HSE GS38). 3. Prove it on a known live source of similar voltage, or on a proving unit made for testers (HSE GS38). With the grid down, use a generator or inverter socket you know is running; a pen may miss a voltage that isn't a clean 50 to 500 Hz sine wave (Klein NCVT7). 4. Test the circuit. A pen needs to be held in your bare hand with the tip within about 6 mm of the wire. It will not detect if you are isolated from an effective earth ground, and may miss through a glove (Klein NCVT7); insulating footwear or a ladder can do that (Bosch GVD 1000-17). 5. Prove it again on the same live source: a tester that failed mid-test gives a false dead (IHSA multimeters; HSE GS38). 6. A silent pen never proves dead (Fluke 1AC II; HSE GS38). Switch off, then prove dead with a two-pole tester or a meter: prove it on a live source as in steps 3 and 5, with the circuit tested in between, neutral and earth too (HSE GS38; ESA Flash 19-03-FL; IHSA multimeters). Never assume neutral or earth wires are dead: neutrals can stay live (Klein NCVT7). Fail signs: nothing on the known live source, or no power light.

decay.note: Estimate. No sensor wears out, but alkaline cells left in can leak and damage the pen or make a shock hazard, so take them out for storage (Fluke 1AC II; Klein NCVT7). Cracked cases and perished leads retire it (HSE GS38). Fresh cells revive most.

improvise: Without a tester, treat every wire as live. Switch off and lock off every source you can find, including generators, inverters and solar. A multimeter, proved on a known live source before and after, can stand in for a two-pole tester, though HSE prefers a two-pole detector or proper test lamp for this job (HSE GS38). Check its marked voltage and CAT rating suit the circuit (HSE GS38; IHSA multimeters). Set it to voltage (DC volts for DC) before you connect and check the leads are in the volt sockets: wrongly set multimeters and makeshift testers have often caused accidents (HSE GS38; IHSA multimeters). A lamp you know works shows a socket is live, but a lamp that stays dark proves nothing, because a broken lamp also stays dark (HSE GS38). Useless or worse: a homemade test lamp of a bulb holder and two bare-ended wires, which HSE lists as a cause of shocks (HSE GS38); a non-contact pen used alone to call a circuit dead (Fluke 1AC II), especially on metal-armoured cable: Klein warns of shielded wire and grounded metal conduit (Klein NCVT7), and a metal sheath may hide the field too, which is our inference, not something either maker says; and assuming a neutral or earth wire is safe (Klein NCVT7). Nothing here is rated for grid lines, substations or other high voltage: stay away from them (HSE GS38 covers up to 1,000 V AC only). Solar arrays, battery banks and EV packs are DC: most pens read nothing there, so use a tester or meter marked for DC and above the system's voltage (Klein NCVT7; HSE GS38), and leave EV packs and large arrays to someone trained.
